n: Odenwaldschule, Heppenheim — abuse by headmaster Gerold Becker and teachers
who: Odenwaldschule (private, state-recognised progressive boarding school); headmaster Gerold Becker, music teacher Wolfgang Held
d: A final report by lawyers Claudia Burgsmüller and Brigitte Tilmann, released 17 December 2010, found that at least 132 pupils were abused by teachers between 1965 and 1998. Former headmaster Gerold Becker and music teacher Wolfgang Held were named as the main perpetrators; the victims' association says at least 20 teachers were involved. The abuse became widely public in 2010; the school closed in September 2015 after insolvency. Becker also appears in the Hildesheim research as a figure in the Kentler network.
cover: After victims came forward in 1998 and the Frankfurter Rundschau reported it in November 1999, a promised review did not take place; prosecutors in Darmstadt dropped the case under the statute of limitations. Becker died in 2010 without facing legal consequences.
cite: Burgsmüller & Tilmann, Abschlussbericht Odenwaldschule, 17 Dec 2010 (via Wikipedia index); News4teachers 2014

n: Grandview Training School for Girls, Galt, Ontario
who: Ontario provincial training school for girls (juvenile reformatory)
d: Former residents of this provincial reform school for girls aged 12–18 alleged physical, sexual and psychological abuse by staff. The abuse became public in 1991, prompting a joint Ontario Provincial Police and Waterloo Regional Police investigation; a survivors' group of more than 300 women sought collective compensation. In 1999 MPP Jim Flaherty apologised in the Ontario legislature on the province's behalf.
cover: Complaints of serious sexual abuse made by girls while at the school were reportedly ignored and never investigated.
cite: Wikipedia (index), citing Legislative Assembly of Ontario Hansard, 19 Nov 1999, and Kaufman report 'Searching for Justice'

n: Parramatta Training School for Girls and Hay Institution — Royal Commission Case Study 7
who: NSW state child-welfare department; Parramatta Girls Home (Parramatta Training School for Girls), Hay Institution for Girls
d: Parramatta Girls Home was a NSW state-run institution for girls from 1887 to 1974, many of them Aboriginal girls of the Stolen Generations. The Royal Commission's February 2014 hearing (Case Study 7, report October 2014) heard evidence about 11 men, most of them superintendents or deputies, accused of physical and sexual abuse. Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated and no criminal charges were laid. A 2004 Senate inquiry had earlier taken statements from 20 former residents.
cover: Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated; some resigned or were dismissed after inquiries; no criminal charges were laid.
cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Report of Case Study No. 7, October 2014 (via Wikipedia)

n: Bringing Them Home — Stolen Generations inquiry
who: Commonwealth, state and territory governments; church and state institutions, foster and adoptive families
d: The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission inquiry, led by Sir Ronald Wilson and Mick Dodson, began in May 1995 and released 'Bringing Them Home' in April 1997. Among 502 inquiry witnesses, 17% of women and 7.7% of men reported sexual assault while in an institution, at work, or in a foster or adoptive family. It found institutions had severe discipline, child labour, poor food and physical and emotional abuse. Prime Minister Kevin Rudd delivered a national apology on 13 February 2008.
cover: The report documented officials misrepresenting capable parents as unfit and telling some parents their children had died when they had not.
cite: Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission, Bringing Them Home, April 1997 (via Wikipedia 'Stolen Generations', citing the report)

n: Forde Inquiry — abuse of children in Queensland institutions
who: 159 government and non-government orphanages, reformatories and detention centres in Queensland
d: The Commission of Inquiry into Abuse of Children in Queensland Institutions, chaired by former governor Leneen Forde, was set up on 13 August 1998 and reported in May 1999. It examined 159 institutions from 1911 to 1999, found that abuse had occurred and made 42 recommendations. Some findings were sealed because matters were still before the courts. It led to state apologies, the Queensland Government Redress Scheme and the Forde Foundation.
cite: Commission of Inquiry into Abuse of Children in Queensland Institutions (Forde Inquiry), May 1999 (via Wikipedia and Qld Government)

n: Mullighan Inquiry — Children in State Care, South Australia
who: South Australian state guardianship system (Families SA and predecessors)
d: Commissioner Ted Mullighan's inquiry began in November 2004 and was widened in 2007 to children on the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands. Its March 2008 report found 'that in the past 65 years the State has failed to protect some of the children in its care from sexual abuse' and that record-keeping on 924 children who died in state care was manifestly inadequate. It made 54 recommendations, and 400 suspected abusers were reported to South Australia Police.
cite: Children in State Care Commission of Inquiry (Mullighan Report), March 2008 (via Wikipedia)

n: Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory (Don Dale)
who: Northern Territory Government youth detention and child protection systems
d: After ABC Four Corners' 'Australia's Shame' aired on 25 July 2016 showing boys at Don Dale assaulted, stripped and tear-gassed, and a boy hooded and shackled in a restraint chair, a Royal Commission was set up on 28 July 2016. Its report, tabled on 17 November 2017, made 142 findings and 226 recommendations, including closing Don Dale. The High Court ruled in June 2020 that the 2014 tear-gassing was unlawful. The Corrections Minister was sacked the morning after the broadcast.
cover: A 2014 media release falsely said six boys had escaped when CCTV showed one; two earlier reports (January 2015 review and the August 2015 Children's Commissioner report) were not acted on.
cite: Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory, final report, 17 November 2017 (via Wikipedia)

n: Scouts Australia — Royal Commission and convictions
who: Scouts Australia (NSW branch, Scouts Victoria)
d: Former NSW Branch Commissioner Roderick Corrie was jailed for seven years in February 2000 after pleading guilty to eight of 77 charges of sexually abusing children as young as 11 between 1969 and 1995. A 1981 internal report on his abuse of four boys had not been referred to police. Other Scout leaders were convicted in Victoria, including Neville Budge in 2017 for abusing eight boys between 1995 and 2002. Scouts Australia was called before the Royal Commission over its handling of complaints.
cover: A 14-page 1981 report by a senior Scout leader detailing allegations against NSW Branch Commissioner Roderick Corrie was not properly investigated or referred to police; Scouts Australia's head apologised in 2000.
cite: Sydney Morning Herald reporting (2000) and Victorian court reports, via Wikipedia 'Scouts Australia'

n: Scouting Ireland — 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review' (Elliott)
who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (CBSI) and Scout Association of Ireland (SAI), merged as Scouting Ireland in 2004
d: Safeguarding expert Ian Elliott's learning review, published by Scouting Ireland in May 2020, identified at least 275 known or suspected sex offenders in CBSI and SAI, mainly from the 1960s to the 1990s. It found a culture 'driven by self-interest', cronyism, and cover-up. Scouting Ireland accepted the findings and apologised; allegations against living people were passed to the Gardaí and Tusla.
cover: The review found 'coverup and a failure to report abuse'; records were lost or destroyed; adults with a sexual interest in young people rose to positions of influence and prevented known offenders being removed.
cite: Ian Elliott, 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review', published May 2020; RTÉ News 14 May 2020 (via Wikipedia)

n: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding
who: Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital, child and adolescent unit; psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks
d: Children in the unit in the 1970s were given electric shocks without anaesthetic and paraldehyde injections as punishment; survivors also reported sexual abuse. The government apologised in 2001 and paid NZ$10.7 million to 183 former patients. Survivors took complaints to the UN Committee Against Torture in 2019. Police announced charges in 2021; psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks was found unfit to stand trial and died in January 2022. In December 2024 the government set redress of at least NZ$150,000 per survivor after the Royal Commission's Lake Alice findings.
cover: The Crown's internal policy refused to recognise the long-term effects of abuse, forcing complaints to the UN Committee Against Torture in 2019.
cite: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, Lake Alice hearing (June 2021); RNZ 18 December 2024; NZ Police release 2021 (via Wikipedia)

n: Muzaffarpur shelter home — TISS audit and convictions
who: Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti (state-funded NGO run by Brajesh Thakur); Bihar Social Welfare Department
d: A social audit of Bihar shelter homes by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, submitted in April 2018, flagged sexual abuse at the Muzaffarpur girls' home; an FIR followed on 31 May 2018. Medical examination confirmed sexual abuse of 34 of the 42 girls. The Supreme Court took suo motu cognizance on 2 August 2018 and moved the case to a Delhi POCSO court, which in January 2020 convicted Brajesh Thakur and 18 others; Thakur was sentenced to life imprisonment.
cover: The then district child protection officer was among the accused; Bihar Social Welfare Minister Manju Verma resigned over the case; the Supreme Court criticised the state for funding the NGO and moved the trial to Delhi. CBI cleared Verma and her husband, a finding disputed by The Caravan.
cite: Tata Institute of Social Sciences audit (2018); Saket POCSO court judgment, January 2020; Firstpost, The Hindu, Indian Express (via Wikipedia)

n: Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción — abuse, trafficking alerts and fire killing 41 girls
who: State-run children's home under the Secretariat of Social Welfare (SBS); National Civil Police
d: The state home, built for 350–500, held 700–800 children in 2017. A contractor was convicted in 2014 of raping a disabled 17-year-old resident and two teachers were arrested for sexual assault. After a protest and escape on 7 March 2017, 51 girls were locked in a schoolroom; a fire broke out the next morning and 41 died. The Secretary of Social Welfare, his deputy and the home's director were arrested on 13 March 2017; on 12 August 2025 former secretary Carlos Rodas and five other officials were convicted of manslaughter and abuse of authority and sentenced to up to 25 years.
cover: Officials ignored repeated complaints: in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for precautionary measures citing mistreatment and a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On the day of the fire police guarding the locked room did not let the girls out.
cite: Guatemala Human Rights Ombudsman (PDH) request to IACHR, Nov 2016; IACHR press release 031/2017; Guatemalan court verdict 12 August 2025 (via Wikipedia)

n: Casitas del Sur — children missing from church-run shelters
who: Iglesia Cristiana Restaurada (Restored Christian Church) shelters; Mexico City Attorney General's Office (PGJDF), which placed children there
d: Children placed by Mexico City prosecutors in the private Casitas del Sur shelter went missing; in October 2008 officials were refused entry when trying to recover a girl whose release a judge had ordered. On 29 January 2009 police and human rights staff removed 126 children; seven staff were charged with obstruction of justice. The missing children were alleged to have been taken for illegal adoption or trafficking, and the federal Attorney General offered a reward for information.
cover: A Mexico City legislator accused officials of the District Attorney's office of negligence and complicity, saying they warned the shelter of searches so children could be moved.
cite: Mexican federal Attorney General reward notice; UN Human Rights Council doc A/HRC/14/32/Add.1; CNN México 2012 (via Wikipedia)

n: Élan School, Poland, Maine — troubled-teen programme
who: Élan School (private behaviour-modification boarding school; NATSAP member)
d: Élan operated from 1970 until 1 April 2011, when it closed after decades of abuse reports from former students. Illinois officials removed eleven children in 1975 alleging mistreatment, and in 2007 New York education officials, who paid tuition for special-education students, alleged students were made to restrain peers and were sleep-deprived. The New Yorker (2000) and Time (2011) described 'the ring', in which students were made to fight one another. Maine State Police reopened the 1982 death of a 15-year-old student in 2016 but filed no charges. The record of sexual abuse rests on former students' accounts; no official sexual-abuse finding was located.
cover: In the late 1970s staff refused a sheriff's lieutenant entry past the lobby after rumours of abuse.
cite: New Yorker (2000); Time (2011); Lewiston Sun Journal; Maine State Police 2016 (via Wikipedia)

n: Provo Canyon School, Utah — licences revoked 2026
who: Provo Canyon School, owned by Universal Health Services (2000–2026)
d: Provo Canyon School, a for-profit residential treatment centre owned by Universal Health Services, faced public accounts from former students including Paris Hilton (2020) of physical abuse, forced medication, strip-searches and seclusion. In June 2026 Utah's Department of Health and Human Services found staff failed to protect a resident during an assault and delayed medical treatment, and on 17 July 2026 revoked the licences of both campuses; UHS appealed. No official sexual-abuse finding was located; the licence revocation concerned failure to protect and safety.
cite: Utah Department of Health and Human Services licence action, June–July 2026; Salt Lake Tribune, 27 July 2026 (via Wikipedia)

n: Romanian state orphanages under Ceaușescu and after 1989
who: Romanian state orphanages and institutions for disabled children
d: Decree 770 (1966) banned abortion, and many children born afterwards were abandoned in state institutions, where they suffered neglect, physical and sexual abuse and sedation; physical and sexual abuse was reported to be common at the Siret children's psychiatric hospital. After 1989 large numbers of children were adopted abroad amid corruption and irregularities, and in 2004, under EU pressure, Romania banned international adoption except by grandparents. A 2009 BBC investigation found poor conditions persisted in some institutions.
cite: Wikipedia 'Romanian orphans' (citing BBC 2009 and academic sources)

n: Mogilino home for children with disabilities, Bulgaria
who: Bulgarian state institution for children with physical and mental disabilities
d: The BBC film 'Bulgaria's Abandoned Children' (2007, Kate Blewett) documented neglect of disabled children at the Mogilino state home. On 22 February 2008 Bulgaria's Labour and Social Policy Minister repeated a promise to close Mogilino and six similar homes, and by June 2008 children were being moved, with UNICEF working towards closure. Bulgaria has been criticised for having one of the highest numbers of children in state institutions in the EU. No sexual-abuse finding was located; this is a neglect record.
cite: BBC, 'Bulgaria's Abandoned Children' (2007); Sofia Echo, 27 June 2008 (via Wikipedia)

n: Gwangju Inhwa School for the deaf — the 'Dogani' case
who: Gwangju Inhwa School for deaf students (founded 1961; principal was the founder's son)
d: A 2005 investigation found six teachers, including the principal, sexually molested or raped at least nine deaf students between 2000 and 2003. Four received prison terms but appeal courts reduced them; two escaped prosecution because of the statute of limitations. After the 2011 film 'Silenced' (Dogani), police reopened the case, the school closed in November 2011, and parliament unanimously passed the 'Dogani Bill' removing the statute of limitations for sex crimes against children under 13 and disabled women. In July 2012 a former administrator was sentenced to 12 years for an April 2005 sexual assault on a student. Whether all victims were boarders was not confirmed.
cover: The teacher who alerted human rights groups in 2005 was fired; police acted only four months later after former students went to national TV; the city government and school board passed the case back and forth; appeal courts cut sentences to probation and four of the six teachers were reinstated.
cite: Korea Times, 4 and 17 October 2011; Gwangju District Court, July 2012 (via Wikipedia)

n: Jean-Luc Brunel — Paris investigation into rape of minors (died before trial)
who: Jean-Luc Brunel; MC2 Model Management (New York/Miami), Karin Models
d: The Paris prosecutor opened an investigation on 23 Aug 2019 into rape and sexual assault of minors and criminal conspiracy linked to Epstein. Model agent Jean-Luc Brunel, whose MC2 agency was reportedly launched in 2005 with up to US$1 million from Epstein, was arrested at Charles de Gaulle airport on 16 Dec 2020 while about to fly to Dakar. He was charged in June 2021 with raping a 17-year-old in the 1990s and later with rape of minors and sexual harassment. He was found hanged in La Santé prison on 19 Feb 2022; a 2023 inquiry ruled suicide. He denied wrongdoing and was never tried.
cite: Wikipedia 'Jean-Luc Brunel' (citing AFP, Le Monde, Paris prosecutor statements)

n: US Virgin Islands government suits — Epstein estate and JPMorgan
who: Epstein estate; JPMorgan Chase; Deutsche Bank
d: Epstein bought Little St. James through L.S.J. LLC in April 1998; FBI agents searched it in August 2019. The USVI Attorney General sued the estate, which agreed in late 2022 to a $105m settlement, the largest in the territory's history. On 27 Dec 2022 USVI sued JPMorgan, alleging it knowingly facilitated Epstein's sex trafficking; JPMorgan settled with victims for $290m (June 2023) and with USVI for $75m (Sept 2023). The settlements carried no criminal findings.
cover: Banks were alleged to have facilitated and concealed the operation by keeping Epstein as a client. New York's financial regulator fined Deutsche Bank $150m in July 2020 for ignoring red flags on Epstein. UK regulators permanently banned former JPMorgan banker Jes Staley (upheld June 2025) for recklessly misleading them about his Epstein relationship.
cite: Wikipedia 'Denise George', 'Jes Staley', 'Deutsche Bank', 'Little Saint James' (citing Reuters, NYT)

n: Thorbjørn Jagland — charged with aggravated corruption over Epstein ties
who: Thorbjørn Jagland (former Norwegian PM, Council of Europe Secretary General, Nobel Committee chair)
d: After the 2026 DOJ releases, Økokrim investigated whether Jagland received gifts, travel or loans from Epstein while chairing the Nobel Committee and leading the Council of Europe. The Council of Europe waived his immunity on 11 Feb 2026 and he was charged with aggravated corruption on 12 Feb 2026; properties were searched. He denies wrongdoing. This is a corruption case, not an abuse charge; recorded for the network's political reach.
cite: Wikipedia 'Thorbjørn Jagland' (citing NRK, CNN, Reuters)

n: Epstein Files Transparency Act and DOJ releases (2025–2026)
who: US Department of Justice; FBI; House Oversight Committee
d: A July 2025 DOJ/FBI memo said there was no 'client list', no credible evidence of blackmail and no basis to investigate uncharged third parties, and affirmed suicide. Congress then passed the Act 427–1 (House) and by unanimous consent (Senate); it was signed 19 Nov 2025. DOJ released files on 19–23 Dec 2025, about 3 million more pages on 30 Jan 2026, and restored about 50,000 removed files on 5 Mar 2026. The releases documented Epstein's continued contact with prominent people after 2008 and led to police inquiries in the UK and Norway and resignations in several countries; they did not establish a client list or prove claims that Epstein 'lent out' girls to powerful men, which FBI notes said other victims did not corroborate. The House Oversight Committee separately obtained the estate's 50th-birthday album from 8 Sept 2025.
cover: DOJ said it identified about 6 million potentially responsive pages but released about 3.5 million, withholding about 200,000 under privilege, abuse material and victim-identity grounds; critics in both parties said it broke the law. Faulty redactions exposed at least 43 victims' names (WSJ). The DOJ Inspector General opened a compliance review in April 2026.
cite: Wikipedia 'Epstein Files Transparency Act' and 'Epstein files' (citing NPR, CNN, DOJ statements); CBS News, 30 Jan 2026

n: Claims that Epstein was tied to intelligence services
who: Claims about US and Israeli intelligence (unproven)
d: In July 2019 journalist Vicky Ward (Daily Beast) cited an anonymous former White House official saying Acosta told transition vetters he had been told Epstein 'belonged to intelligence' and to leave it alone. Acosta denied this, and DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility (Nov 2020) found no evidence Epstein was a cooperating witness or intelligence asset. Former Israeli intelligence figure Ari Ben-Menashe has claimed Robert Maxwell (Ghislaine's father) was a Mossad agent; Congress's Iran-Contra investigators called his testimony 'not credible'. Documented: Epstein had a close business relationship with former Israeli PM Ehud Barak (investment in Reporty/Carbyne, about 30 visits 2013–2017); Barak denies wrongdoing. No official body has found that Epstein worked for any intelligence service.
cite: Wikipedia 'Alexander Acosta' (citing Daily Beast, 9 Jul 2019, and OPR report Nov 2020); Wikipedia 'Ari Ben-Menashe'; Wikipedia 'Ehud Barak'

n: Jimmy Savile — 'Giving Victims a Voice' (Met Police/NSPCC)
who: Jimmy Savile (BBC broadcaster); BBC; NHS hospitals; Metropolitan Police
d: After Savile's death in October 2011, an ITV documentary on 3 Oct 2012 carried accounts of abuse of teenage girls. The Metropolitan Police opened Operation Yewtree on 19 Oct 2012. The January 2013 Met/NSPCC report 'Giving Victims a Voice' recorded 214 crimes, including 34 rape or penetration offences. The scandal was a major reason for creating the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA).
cover: Earliest known police report dates from 1958, with police intelligence from 1963; Surrey Police investigated in 2007–09 without charges. A BBC Newsnight investigation was shelved in December 2011; the Pollard Review called the decision flawed.
cite: Metropolitan Police & NSPCC, 'Giving Victims a Voice', Jan 2013 (via Wikipedia 'Jimmy Savile sexual abuse scandal')

n: Dame Janet Smith Review — Savile and Stuart Hall at the BBC
who: BBC
d: The independent review by Dame Janet Smith, published in February 2016, found that Savile sexually abused 72 people in connection with his BBC work, raping eight, the youngest aged eight. It found that Stuart Hall assaulted at least 21 girls and women at the BBC, the youngest aged 10. Some staff knew of complaints, but these were not escalated.
cover: Some BBC staff knew of complaints about Savile and Hall but did not pass them to senior management; Hall's celebrity status discouraged staff from escalating.
cite: Dame Janet Smith Review, Feb 2016 (via Wikipedia 'Jimmy Savile sexual abuse scandal' and 'Stuart Hall (presenter)')

n: Lampard report — Savile in NHS hospitals
who: NHS hospitals (Leeds General Infirmary, Stoke Mandeville, Broadmoor and others)
d: Kate Lampard's investigation (reports June 2014 and February 2015) summarised 44 NHS investigations and found Savile abused patients, staff and visitors aged 5 to 75 in NHS hospitals, where his celebrity and fundraising gave him keys and access. At Leeds General Infirmary 60 people said they were abused.
cite: Kate Lampard, 'Themes and lessons learnt from NHS investigations into matters relating to Jimmy Savile', Feb 2015 (via Wikipedia)

n: Cyril Smith MP — Cambridge House and Knowl View, Rochdale
who: Cyril Smith (Liberal MP for Rochdale 1972–1992); Lancashire Constabulary; Director of Public Prosecutions; Rochdale Council
d: Cyril Smith was alleged to have sexually and physically abused teenage boys at the Cambridge House hostel he co-founded in Rochdale in the 1960s and at Knowl View school. He died in 2010, never charged. In November 2012 Greater Manchester Police cited 'overwhelming evidence' of abuse of young boys. The IICSA report on Cambridge House, Knowl View and Rochdale (April 2018) examined why he was never prosecuted; Rochdale Council removed his Freedom of the Borough in October 2018.
cover: Police evidence presented in 1970 led to no action; the CPS said in 2012 that Smith should have been charged and that he had been given an assurance in 1970 he would not be prosecuted. Press allegations in 1979 (Rochdale Alternative Press, Private Eye) produced no prosecution. He was knighted in 1988 though Margaret Thatcher had been told of the allegations.
cite: IICSA, 'Cambridge House, Knowl View and Rochdale' investigation report, April 2018; CPS statement Nov 2012 (via Wikipedia 'Cyril Smith')

n: Elm Guest House, London — VIP-abuse claims
who: Elm Guest House; Metropolitan Police (Operation Fernbridge)
d: Police raided the guest house in 1982 and the owners were charged with running a disorderly house. Claims from 1990 onward that politicians visited were investigated in Operation Fernbridge (2013–2015); its prosecutions did not expose abuse linked to Elm. At IICSA in 2019 Commander Neil Jerome said that, apart from a child removed during the raid, no credible victim had alleged an offence there and no prominent person was conclusively identified. A 10-year-old boy removed in the raid had been raped, so abuse occurred; the VIP claims are unsupported.
cite: IICSA Westminster hearings, Feb 2019 (via Wikipedia 'Elm Guest House')

n: Operation Midland — Carl Beech's false 'VIP ring' claims
who: Metropolitan Police; Carl Beech (complainant)
d: Between November 2014 and March 2016 the Met investigated Carl Beech's claims that a VIP ring of politicians and generals abused boys and committed murders, including at Dolphin Square. It searched homes and named suspects, including Leon Brittan, Harvey Proctor and Lord Bramall, but charged no one. Sir Richard Henriques's review (Nov 2016) found the accused were victims of false allegations. In July 2019 Beech was convicted of perverting the course of justice and fraud and, separately, of child sexual offences including indecent images; he was jailed for 18 years.
cite: Henriques review, Nov 2016; Newcastle Crown Court, July 2019 (via Wikipedia 'Operation Midland')

n: Rolf Harris — convicted of indecent assault of girls
who: Rolf Harris (entertainer)
d: Arrested in March 2013 under Operation Yewtree, Harris was found guilty on 30 June 2014 of 12 counts of indecent assault against four girls and young women between the 1960s and 1986, one aged eight. He was sentenced to five years nine months. In 2017 the Court of Appeal quashed one conviction; the other 11 stood. He died in 2023.
cite: Southwark Crown Court, 30 Jun & 4 Jul 2014 (via Wikipedia 'Rolf Harris')

n: Gary Glitter (Paul Gadd) — UK, Cambodia and Vietnam cases
who: Paul Gadd ('Gary Glitter', pop singer)
d: Convicted in the UK in 1999 of possessing over 4,000 child abuse images (4 months). He was expelled from Cambodia in 2002–03. In 2006 a Vietnamese court convicted him of obscene acts with two girls aged 10 and 11 (3 years). In 2015, after Operation Yewtree, he was convicted of attempted rape and indecent assault of three girls in 1975–1980 and sentenced to 16 years; recalled to prison in March 2023.
cite: Wikipedia 'Gary Glitter' (citing court reports)

n: Stuart Hall — indecent assault of girls (BBC presenter)
who: Stuart Hall (BBC broadcaster)
d: In April 2013 Hall pleaded guilty to 14 counts of indecent assault on 13 girls aged 9 to 17; his 15-month sentence was doubled to 30 months as unduly lenient. In May 2014 he was convicted of two more counts involving a 13-year-old (total five years).
cite: Preston Crown Court 2013–14 (via Wikipedia 'Stuart Hall (presenter)')

n: Max Clifford — indecent assault
who: Max Clifford (publicist)
d: Clifford was convicted in April 2014 of eight counts of indecent assault against four victims aged 15 to 19 and jailed for eight years; his appeal failed. He died in prison in December 2017.
cite: Wikipedia 'Max Clifford'

n: Operation Yewtree — post-Savile investigation of public figures
who: Metropolitan Police
d: Launched on 19 Oct 2012, Yewtree arrested 19 people by Oct 2015; seven were convicted (Gadd, Dave Lee Travis on one count, Clifford, Harris, Chris Denning, Michael Salmon, Geoffrey Wheeler). Others were acquitted or never charged, including several well-known names, and must not be described as offenders.
cite: Wikipedia 'Operation Yewtree'

n: Huw Edwards — indecent images of children
who: Huw Edwards (BBC newsreader)
d: BBC newsreader Huw Edwards was arrested on 8 Nov 2023 and pleaded guilty on 31 July 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children, received via WhatsApp (41 of 377 images sent by another man were indecent images of children). On 16 Sept 2024 he received six months suspended for two years.
cover: The BBC kept paying him after his November 2023 arrest; it later asked him to repay over £200,000.
cite: Wikipedia 'Huw Edwards' (citing BBC, CPS)

n: Barry Bennell and English youth football (Sheldon Review)
who: Barry Bennell (coach/scout, Crewe Alexandra, Manchester City links); The Football Association
d: Bennell was convicted in Florida in 1994 (abuse of a 13-year-old club player), at Chester in 1998 (23 offences, six boys), in 2015, in Feb 2018 (50 offences against 12 boys; 31 years) and in 2020. After former player Andy Woodward spoke out in Nov 2016 more than 350 alleged victims came forward within a month. Clive Sheldon QC's review (17 Mar 2021) criticised the FA and eight clubs. By end-2021, 14 men had been convicted. Bennell died in prison in 2023.
cover: Crewe Alexandra heard an allegation but kept Bennell on with restrictions (former director Hamilton Smith). The Sheldon Review found the FA guilty of 'institutional failure' for delaying safeguards after 1995.
cite: Sheldon Independent Review, 17 Mar 2021; Wikipedia 'Barry Bennell'

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — elite boarding schools (Fettes, Loretto, Gordonstoun, Edinburgh Academy, Merchiston)
who: Fettes College, Loretto School, Gordonstoun, Edinburgh Academy, Merchiston Castle School
d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry found or heard admissions of sexual abuse at elite independent schools: Fettes accepted Iain Wares molested junior boys in 1973–79; Loretto admitted abuse by a teacher in the 1950s–60s; at Gordonstoun 11 alleged abuse incidents included the rape of a 13-year-old girl by an instructor; Merchiston admitted abuse between 1930 and 2014. The inquiry estimated about three quarters of children in Wares's Edinburgh Academy classes were abused. South Africa approved Wares's extradition, which he was still fighting in 2025.
cover: Fettes dismissed teacher Iain Wares in 1979 but gave him a glowing testimonial; he went on to teach in South Africa.
cite: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry boarding-school case study findings, 2021–2023 (via Wikipedia 'Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry' and 'Edinburgh Academy')

n: Dutroux affair — kidnap, abuse and murder of girls; police and justice failures
who: Marc Dutroux, Michelle Martin, Michel Lelièvre; Belgian Gendarmerie and judicial police
d: Dutroux kidnapped six girls in 1995–96; four died. He was arrested on 13 Aug 1996; about 300,000 people joined the White March on 20 Oct 1996. The Verwilghen parliamentary commission (Feb 1998) found 'corruption, carelessness and incompetence' but no high-level protectors. On 22 June 2004 he was sentenced to life; Martin got 30 years and Lelièvre 25; businessman Michel Nihoul was acquitted of kidnapping and convicted on drug charges. Belgium reorganised its police forces.
cover: Dutroux was released early in 1992 from a 13.5-year sentence over prosecutor and psychiatrist objections. Police missed chances, including voices heard in his cellar and unreviewed videotapes; rivalry between Gendarmerie and judicial police hampered the hunt. Judge Connerotte was removed in Oct 1996 for attending a victims' fundraising dinner.
cite: Verwilghen parliamentary commission, Feb 1998; Arlon assize court, 22 Jun 2004 (via Wikipedia 'Marc Dutroux')

n: Dutroux 'X-dossiers' — witness claims of an elite abuse network
who: Witnesses X1–X4 (claims); Belgian prosecutors
d: Witnesses including Régina Louf told investigators in 1996–97 of abuse parties and unsolved murders involving Dutroux and Nihoul and prominent people. Prosecutors ultimately dismissed her statements, and investigators were criticised for leading her; an officer charged in 1997 with falsifying her statements was cleared in 1999. The parliamentary commission found no high-level protectors. The claims remain unproven; a 1999 book by three journalists argued the witnesses were more credible than portrayed.
cite: Wikipedia 'Marc Dutroux' (citing Verwilghen commission and press)

n: Casa Pia — abuse of children in state care by a TV presenter, diplomat and others
who: Casa Pia (state children's institution); Carlos Cruz (TV presenter); Jorge Ritto (ex-ambassador); Hugo Marçal (lawyer); Ferreira Diniz (doctor); Manuel Abrantes (Casa Pia official); Carlos Silvino (driver)
d: The scandal broke in Sept–Nov 2002 (Felícia Cabrita, Expresso). After a trial from 2004, on 3 Sept 2010 six men were convicted: driver Carlos Silvino (18 years), TV presenter Carlos Cruz (7), doctor Ferreira Diniz (7), ex-ambassador Jorge Ritto (6y8m), lawyer Hugo Marçal (6y2m) and Casa Pia official Manuel Abrantes (5y9m). Former minister Paulo Pedroso was detained but charges were dropped and he won €100,000 for wrongful detention.
cover: A teacher reportedly began reporting abuse to Casa Pia leaders and police in 1975, and police accused a caretaker in 1981, without legal action. Ritto had been removed as consul in Stuttgart around 1969–71 after a complaint about an under-age boy, but stayed in the diplomatic service.
cite: Lisbon criminal court verdict, 3 Sept 2010 (via Wikipedia 'Casa Pia child sexual abuse scandal')

n: Joris Demmink allegations (Netherlands) — investigated, never charged
who: Allegations against the former Secretary-General of the Dutch Ministry of Justice
d: In 2007 an imprisoned Turkish man alleged that Demmink raped two boys in Turkey in the late 1990s; a criminal complaint followed in 2010. An appeals court ordered an investigation in January 2014; in June 2016 prosecutors said it produced no reliable evidence, and it was discontinued in 2017 (no evidence he was in Turkey; Turkey did not cooperate). Demmink was never charged and denies the allegations.
cite: Wikipedia 'Joris Demmink' (citing Dutch Public Prosecution Service, NOS)

n: Gabriel Matzneff — writer's published accounts of abusing minors
who: Gabriel Matzneff (author); French literary establishment (Gallimard and others)
d: Vanessa Springora's 'Le Consentement' (late 2019/Jan 2020) described his relationship with her at 14. Gallimard withdrew his books in January 2020, and Paris prosecutors opened an investigation for rape of a minor under 15; police searched Gallimard on 12 Feb 2020. The case was dismissed because the statute of limitations had expired.
cover: Literary tolerance: Matzneff published diaries describing sex with minors and child sex tourism in the Philippines (e.g. 1985) and was celebrated on TV (Apostrophes, 1990).
cite: Wikipedia 'Gabriel Matzneff' (citing Le Monde, AFP)

n: Olivier Duhamel — incest allegation ('La Familia grande')
who: Olivier Duhamel (constitutional scholar, head of Sciences Po foundation FNSP)
d: In January 2021 Camille Kouchner's book alleged that Duhamel abused her twin brother, his 13-year-old stepson, in 1988. Paris prosecutors opened an investigation on 5 Jan 2021; Duhamel resigned his posts. In April 2021 French media, citing sources close to the investigation, reported he admitted the abuse. The facts were time-barred.
cite: Wikipedia 'Olivier Duhamel' (citing Le Monde, AFP)

n: Joël Le Scouarnec — surgeon convicted for 299 victims
who: Joël Le Scouarnec (surgeon); hospitals and medical regulators
d: Le Scouarnec, a surgeon in western France, was convicted in Saintes in Dec 2020 of raping and assaulting four children (15 years). On 28 May 2025 the Vannes court convicted him of offences against 299 victims, mostly hospital patients under 15, between 1989 and 2014, and imposed the maximum 20 years. He is not part of an elite network; included as a professional whose standing protected him (setting is debatable — could be moved to 'care').
cover: The FBI traced his downloading of abuse images in 2004; his 2005 conviction (4 months suspended) brought no restriction on practice. Prosecutors did not alert medical authorities; the regional medical body found no breach in 2006; a 2007 warning to the health ministry brought no action; a hospital hired him in 2008 knowing of the conviction.
cite: Vannes criminal court, 28 May 2025 (via Wikipedia 'Joël Le Scouarnec')

n: Hungary — presidential pardon in Bicske children's-home cover-up case
who: President Katalin Novák; Justice Minister Judit Varga; Bicske children's home
d: The pardon became public on 2 Feb 2024. President Novák resigned on 10 Feb 2024 and Justice Minister Varga, who countersigned it, left politics the same day; Reformed Church leader Zoltán Balog resigned on 16 Feb. It is the only case in this set where a head of state resigned over a child-abuse cover-up pardon.
cover: In April 2023 the president pardoned the home's former deputy director, Endre Kónya, who had been convicted of helping cover up the director's sexual abuse of children.
cite: Wikipedia 'Katalin Novák' (citing 444.hu, Reuters)

n: Lord Greville Janner — allegations from Leicestershire children's homes; never tried
who: Greville Janner (Labour MP and peer); Leicestershire Police; Crown Prosecution Service
d: Allegations that Janner abused boys in Leicestershire children's homes were first made in 1991. In April 2015 the CPS decided not to charge him because of dementia; a review reversed this in June 2015, but he was found unfit to plead in Dec 2015 and died on 19 Dec 2015 before a 'trial of the facts'. He was never convicted; the official findings concern the failure of police and prosecutors to act.
cover: Police investigated in 1991, 2002 and 2007 without charges. The Henriques report (Jan 2016) found the CPS and police at fault and said a prosecution was likely to have succeeded in 1991, 2002 or 2007. A 2021 review found police 'appeared reluctant to fully investigate'.
cite: Henriques report on CPS/police handling, Jan 2016 (via Wikipedia 'Greville Janner')

n: Lord Nazir Ahmed — convicted of offences against two children in the 1970s
who: Nazir Ahmed (former Labour peer)
d: On 5 Jan 2022 the former peer was convicted of attempted rape of a girl and a serious sexual assault on a boy committed in 1971–1974, when he was a teenager. He was sentenced to 5½ years (reduced to 2½ on appeal in March 2023). He had left the Lords in 2020 over a separate complaint.
cite: Sheffield Crown Court, Jan–Feb 2022 (via Wikipedia 'Nazir Ahmed, Baron Ahmed')

n: Imran Ahmad Khan MP — sexual assault of a 15-year-old boy
who: Imran Ahmad Khan (Conservative MP for Wakefield)
d: A sitting MP, Khan was convicted on 11 Apr 2022 of sexually assaulting a 15-year-old boy in 2008, expelled from the Conservative Party, resigned his seat, and was sentenced to 18 months; his appeal failed in Dec 2022.
cite: Southwark Crown Court, Apr–May 2022 (via Wikipedia 'Imran Ahmad Khan')

n: Sebastian Edathy (Bundestag) — images of naked minors; case closed on payment
who: Sebastian Edathy (SPD member of the Bundestag)
d: Edathy resigned from the Bundestag on 7 Feb 2014; his home and offices were searched on 9 Feb over material bought from a Canadian company. In March 2015 he admitted downloading images and videos of naked minors on his official laptop and the Verden court ended the trial against a €5,000 payment; he has no conviction.
cover: Interior Minister Hans-Peter Friedrich resigned on 14 Feb 2014 after being accused of disclosing the investigation to SPD leaders.
cite: Verden District Court, March 2015 (via Wikipedia 'Sebastian Edathy')

n: Jean Succar Kuri — Cancún child sexual exploitation ring
who: Jean Succar Kuri (hotelier); associates named in Lydia Cacho's reporting
d: Hotel businessman Succar Kuri was detained in Chandler, Arizona in 2004 and extradited to Mexico (2006). On 31 Aug 2011 he was sentenced to 112 years for child pornography and corruption of minors; the conviction was upheld in 2016. He died in Cancún in 2024. Journalist Lydia Cacho's book 'Los demonios del Edén' linked him to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif.
cover: See the related record on journalist Lydia Cacho's 2005 arrest arranged after her book exposed the ring.
cite: Wikipedia 'Jean Succar Kuri' (citing El Universal, CBS)

n: Lydia Cacho's arrest — Puebla governor and businessman protected exploitation ring
who: Mario Marín (Governor of Puebla); Kamel Nacif Borge (businessman)
d: A federal court issued arrest warrants in April 2019 against Marín and Nacif for the torture of Cacho. Marín was arrested in Acapulco on 3 Feb 2021. As of 2023 reporting he remained in custody; his current trial status was not confirmed. Nacif's status was not confirmed.
cover: Intimidation of a journalist: after Cacho exposed the Cancún ring, Puebla police arrested her in Cancún and drove her about 900 miles to Puebla. Leaked calls (La Jornada, 14 Feb 2006) recorded Nacif and Marín discussing jailing her as a favour and having her abused in jail. Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6–4 on 29 Nov 2007 that Marín had no case to answer.
cite: Wikipedia 'Lydia Cacho'; Wikipedia (es) 'Mario Marín Torres' (citing La Jornada, FGR)

n: Spiniak case, Chile — child exploitation ring and false accusation against a senator
who: Claudio Spiniak (businessman)
d: Businessman Claudio Spiniak was arrested on 30 Sept 2003 accused of running a paedophile network; in 2008 the Supreme Court sentenced him to 12 years (later 10) for abusing five minors. Witness Gema Bueno accused Senator Jovino Novoa of attending abuse parties, then admitted in Aug 2004 that she had lied; she and a priest who induced her were convicted of false testimony (upheld 2008). Novoa and other politicians named were cleared — the political-network claim is disproved.
cite: Chilean Supreme Court, 7 Aug 2008 (via Wikipedia (es) 'Caso Spiniak')

n: Larry Nassar — USA Gymnastics and Michigan State University
who: Larry Nassar (team doctor); USA Gymnastics; Michigan State University; FBI; US Olympic & Paralympic Committee
d: Nassar pleaded guilty to federal child-abuse-image charges (60 years, Dec 2017) and was sentenced in Michigan to 40–175 years (Jan 2018) and 40–125 years (Feb 2018). Settlements: Michigan State $500m (2018); USAG and USOPC $380m (Dec 2021); the US government $138.7m over FBI failures (2024). Abuse also occurred at the Karolyi Ranch national training centre in Texas. IndyStar's Sept 2016 investigation triggered the case.
cover: Athletes complained as early as 1997. USAG was told on 17 June 2015. The DOJ Inspector General (July 2021) found FBI agents failed to act on the gymnasts' reports and that supervisory agent W. Jay Abbott later lied about it. MSU dean William Strampel was convicted of misconduct in office (2019); charges against ex-MSU president Lou Anna Simon (dismissed 2020) and ex-USAG CEO Steve Penny (dropped 2022) did not end in convictions; coach Kathie Klages's conviction was overturned (2021). USA Gymnastics had complaints against 54 coaches 1996–2006.
cite: DOJ OIG report on FBI handling of Nassar allegations, July 2021; Wikipedia 'Larry Nassar' and 'USA Gymnastics sex abuse scandal'

n: Jerry Sandusky — Penn State football and The Second Mile
who: Jerry Sandusky (assistant coach); Pennsylvania State University; The Second Mile charity
d: Sandusky was charged in Nov 2011 and convicted on 22 June 2012 of 45 of 48 counts involving 10 boys, then sentenced to 30–60 years. The NCAA fined Penn State $60m. By Nov 2015 Penn State owed close to $93m to victims. Sandusky met boys through The Second Mile charity he founded in 1977.
cover: A 1998 report to Penn State police was not prosecuted. In 2001 graduate assistant Mike McQueary reported seeing Sandusky with a boy in a shower; it went to Joe Paterno, athletic director Tim Curley and vice-president Gary Schultz. The Freeh report (July 2012) found Paterno, president Graham Spanier, Curley and Schultz concealed Sandusky's activities. Curley, Schultz and Spanier were convicted of child endangerment in 2017.
cite: Freeh report, 12 July 2012; Centre County court, 2012 (via Wikipedia 'Penn State child sex abuse scandal')

n: Dennis Hastert — former House Speaker admitted abusing boys he coached
who: Dennis Hastert (Speaker of the US House 1999–2007; former wrestling coach)
d: Hastert was indicted in May 2015 for structuring cash withdrawals and lying to the FBI, and pleaded guilty to structuring in Oct 2015. At sentencing in April 2016 he admitted sexually abusing boys he coached at Yorkville High School (1965–1981); the judge called him a 'serial child molester' and sentenced him to 15 months. He was never convicted of a sexual offence.
cover: Hush money: he withdrew about $952,000 in structured cash payments to a former student; the statute of limitations meant no sex-crime charge was possible.
cite: US District Court, N.D. Illinois, April 2016 (via Wikipedia 'Dennis Hastert')

n: Mark Foley — messages to congressional pages; House leadership 'negligent'
who: Rep. Mark Foley; House Republican leadership
d: In Sept 2006 sexually explicit emails and messages from Rep. Foley to teenage former House pages became public; he resigned on 29 Sept 2006. No criminal charges were brought.
cover: Complaints reached House staff and leaders around 2000–2005. The House Ethics Committee (Dec 2006) found Speaker Hastert and other leaders 'negligent' but recommended no sanctions. Florida's FDLE closed its probe in 2008 citing insufficient evidence and said Congress and Foley denied it access to data.
cite: House Committee on Standards of Official Conduct report, Dec 2006 (via Wikipedia 'Mark Foley scandal')

n: Joel Greenberg conviction and House Ethics findings on Matt Gaetz
who: Joel Greenberg (Seminole County tax collector); Rep. Matt Gaetz (not charged)
d: Greenberg pleaded guilty on 17 May 2021 to sex trafficking of a 17-year-old girl in 2017 and other charges and was sentenced to 11 years (1 Dec 2022). DOJ investigated Rep. Gaetz over the same girl but did not charge him. The House Ethics Committee report (Dec 2024) found evidence Gaetz paid for sex, including with the 17-year-old in 2017, but insufficient evidence of sex trafficking under federal law. Gaetz denies sexual contact with a minor.
cite: US District Court, M.D. Florida; House Ethics Committee report, Dec 2024 (via Wikipedia 'Joel Greenberg (politician)' and 'Matt Gaetz')

n: R. Kelly — racketeering and child sexual abuse material convictions
who: Robert Kelly (singer) and his entourage (racketeering enterprise)
d: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted Kelly on 27 Sept 2021 of racketeering and Mann Act sex-trafficking offences, including against minors (30 years). In 2022 a Chicago federal jury convicted him of producing child sexual abuse material and enticing minors, adding a further sentence in 2023. The 2019 documentary 'Surviving R. Kelly' led to the new prosecutions.
cover: He was acquitted in 2008 of child pornography charges brought in 2002, despite Chicago Sun-Times reporting from 2000.
cite: EDNY and NDIL verdicts 2021–2022 (via Wikipedia 'R. Kelly')

n: Jared Fogle (Subway spokesman) — child abuse material and paid sex with minors
who: Jared Fogle; Russell Taylor (co-conspirator); Subway
d: Arrested on 7 July 2015, Fogle pleaded guilty to distributing and receiving child abuse material and travelling to engage in illicit sexual conduct with a minor, and was sentenced to 15 years 8 months on 19 Nov 2015, with $1.4m restitution to 14 victims.
cover: Allegations surfaced in 2007 but the FBI acted only in 2015. A franchisee says she told Subway in 2008 about Fogle's messages seeking sex with a minor; Subway says it has no record.
cite: US District Court, S.D. Indiana, Nov 2015 (via Wikipedia 'Jared Fogle')

n: Brian Peck — Nickelodeon dialogue coach convicted of abusing a child actor
who: Brian Peck (Nickelodeon dialogue coach)
d: Peck was arrested on 19 Aug 2003 and pleaded no contest in May 2004 to a lewd act on a 14–15-year-old and oral copulation with a minor; he was sentenced to 16 months. The victim, actor Drake Bell, identified himself publicly in the March 2024 documentary 'Quiet on Set'.
cover: Several entertainment-industry figures wrote letters supporting Peck at sentencing in 2004; some apologised in 2024.
cite: Wikipedia 'Brian Peck' (citing LA court records, Investigation Discovery)

n: Roman Polanski — 1977 guilty plea, fugitive since 1978
who: Roman Polanski (film director)
d: Arrested on 10 March 1977 for offences against a 13-year-old girl, Polanski pleaded guilty to unlawful sexual intercourse with a minor. He fled before sentencing and has lived mainly in France. Swiss police detained him in 2009 but Switzerland refused extradition in July 2010; Poland's Supreme Court refused in Dec 2016. A 2023 civil suit alleging rape of a minor in 1973 was settled in 2024.
cover: Fled to France on 1 Feb 1978 before sentencing; Switzerland (2010) and Poland (2015–16) refused US extradition.
cite: Wikipedia 'Roman Polanski sexual abuse case'

n: Michael Jackson — 1993 allegations settled, 2005 acquittal
who: Michael Jackson (singer)
d: A 1993 allegation by a 13-year-old led two grand juries to decline to indict; Jackson settled the family's civil suit in Jan 1994 for a reported $23m without admission. He was charged in Dec 2003 with molesting a 13-year-old and acquitted on all 10 counts on 13 June 2005. No criminal finding exists against him.
cite: Santa Barbara County Superior Court verdict, 13 June 2005 (via Wikipedia 'Trial of Michael Jackson')

n: Graham James — junior hockey coach (Western Hockey League)
who: Graham James (coach/GM, Swift Current Broncos, Calgary Hitmen)
d: James pleaded guilty in Jan 1997 to sexually assaulting two players, including Sheldon Kennedy (3½ years). After Theo Fleury's 2009 memoir and complaint he pleaded guilty in Dec 2011 to assaults on Fleury and Todd Holt; the 2-year sentence was raised to 5 years on appeal in Feb 2013.
cover: He received a federal pardon in 2007, which became public in 2010.
cite: Manitoba Court of Appeal, 15 Feb 2013 (via Wikipedia 'Graham James (ice hockey)')

n: USA Swimming — coaches banned for abuse; claims mishandled
who: USA Swimming
d: USA Swimming banned coach Rick Curl for life in 2012 and former Olympic coach Mitch Ivey in 2013. A 2018 Orange County Register investigation reported hundreds of swimmers whose abuse claims were allegedly mishandled or ignored. Former coach Andy King is serving 40 years after pleading no contest to 20 child molestation charges.
cite: Wikipedia 'USA Swimming' (citing Orange County Register, 2018)

n: Franklin credit union 'child prostitution ring' allegations, Nebraska
who: Claims against Lawrence E. King Jr. (Franklin Community Federal Credit Union) and prominent Nebraskans
d: After federal agents raided the Franklin credit union in Nov 1988 over a $38m embezzlement, claims spread that its manager Lawrence King hosted parties where minors were abused. In July 1990 a Douglas County grand jury called the claims a 'carefully crafted hoax' and indicted two accusers for perjury; a federal grand jury in Sept 1990 also found them unfounded. King pleaded guilty to embezzlement (15 years). A 1999 $1m civil default judgment against King, who did not respond, is not a finding of fact.
cite: Douglas County grand jury report, July 1990 (via Wikipedia 'Franklin child prostitution ring allegations')

n: 'Pizzagate' — false claim of a child-trafficking ring at a Washington pizzeria
who: Online conspiracy theory targeting Democratic politicians
d: In Oct–Nov 2016 online posts claimed Democrats ran a child-abuse ring from Comet Ping Pong, citing leaked Podesta emails. DC police called it 'fictitious'; the restaurant has no basement and no victims or evidence emerged. On 4 Dec 2016 Edgar Maddison Welch fired a rifle inside; he pleaded guilty and was jailed for four years (June 2017).
cite: US District Court for DC, 22 June 2017 (via Wikipedia 'Pizzagate conspiracy theory')

n: McMartin preschool trial — 'satanic abuse' panic ends in acquittals
who: McMartin Preschool (accused: Ray Buckey, Peggy McMartin Buckey)
d: After a 1983 accusation, investigators claimed 360 children had been abused, using interview techniques later judged coercive. Peggy McMartin Buckey was acquitted on all counts in Jan 1990; Ray Buckey was acquitted on 52 counts and two juries deadlocked on the rest, so charges were dropped. There were no convictions after seven years and about $15m. Included as the template for 'ritual abuse' claims; not an elite case strictly.
cite: Wikipedia 'McMartin preschool trial'

n: Johnny Kitagawa — Johnny & Associates talent agency
who: Johnny Kitagawa (founder, Johnny & Associates; now Smile-Up)
d: An independent investigation reported on 29 Aug 2023 that Kitagawa repeatedly sexually abused boys and young men from the early 1970s to the mid-2010s. The company admitted the abuse on 7 Sept 2023, renamed itself Smile-Up and began compensation in Nov 2023. The BBC documentary 'Predator' (March 2023) and Kauan Okamoto's April 2023 testimony triggered the reckoning. Kitagawa died in 2019 and was never charged.
cover: Media silence: Shukan Bunshun's 2001 reports were upheld on the sexual allegations by the courts (damages reduced 2003; Supreme Court rejected appeal 2004), yet Japanese media barely covered them; journalists attributed this to the agency's power over talent bookings. Earliest cited report: Weekly Sankei, 1965.
cite: Johnny & Associates external special investigation team report, 29 Aug 2023 (via Wikipedia 'Johnny Kitagawa' and 'Johnny & Associates')

n: Unnao rape case — MLA Kuldeep Singh Sengar
who: Kuldeep Singh Sengar (BJP MLA, Uttar Pradesh)
d: Sengar raped a 16-year-old girl in June 2017 who came to him seeking a job. He was convicted in Dec 2019 by a Delhi court of kidnapping and raping a minor. On 23 Dec 2025 the Delhi High Court suspended his sentence; the Supreme Court stayed that order on 29 Dec 2025 while it hears the case.
cover: The victim's father died in police custody; in July 2019 a truck crash killed two of her aunts and critically injured her and her lawyer (a court later accepted the CBI finding of no foul play in the crash). The arrest came only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it in 2018.
cite: Wikipedia 'Kuldeep Singh Sengar' (citing Indian Express, The Hindu)

n: Kasur child abuse video scandal (Hussain Khanwala)
who: Local gang filming abuse of children; Punjab police; local MPA (alleged)
d: In August 2015 The Nation reported that a gang in Hussain Khanwala had filmed the abuse of about 280 children between 2006 and 2014 and used the videos to blackmail families. Placed in 'elite' for the alleged political protection; convictions were not verified for this record.
cover: Punjab police and the local PML-N provincial assembly member Malik Ahmad Saeed Khan were alleged to have tried to cover it up; the Punjab law minister called the reports a land dispute. Police clashed with protesting villagers on 8 Aug 2015.
cite: Wikipedia 'Kasur child sexual abuse scandal' (citing The Nation, Aug 2015)

n: Knox Grammar School — headmaster failed to report teachers' abuse
who: Knox Grammar School; Uniting Church
d: In 2009 five former teachers were charged with sex offences from 1976–1990 and all were convicted. The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse held case study 23 in 2015 and reported in Sept 2016.
cover: The Royal Commission (Sept 2016) found headmaster Ian Paterson never reported a student's abuse allegation to police in about 30 years, despite a duty from 1988; he let accused teachers resign and gave some positive references, and withheld information from a police officer.
cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Case Study 23 report, Sept 2016 (via Wikipedia 'Knox Grammar School')

n: Geelong Grammar School — Royal Commission case study 32
who: Geelong Grammar School (Anglican)
d: Former students described abuse by staff between 1956 and 1989 across four campuses. Five former staff were convicted of child sex offences, including a boarding-house assistant who pleaded guilty in 2005 to 41 offences against 40 boys.
cover: The Royal Commission found the school repeatedly failed to investigate or report credible allegations, particularly under principal John Lewis (1980–94), and 'placed its own interests ahead of those of victims'. A 2007 settlement with victims of a boarding-house assistant was minuted as 'a very satisfactory financial outcome for the school'.
cite: Royal Commission Case Study 32 report, 2016–17 (via Wikipedia 'Geelong Grammar School')

n: Brisbane Grammar / St Paul's — counsellor abuse; Governor-General resigns over church handling
who: Brisbane Grammar School; St Paul's School; Anglican Diocese of Brisbane (Archbishop Peter Hollingworth)
d: Lynch, counsellor at Brisbane Grammar 1976–1988, was charged in Jan 1997 and died by suicide the next day. Hollingworth, then Governor-General of Australia, resigned on 26 May 2003 after the diocesan report was tabled in the Queensland parliament. The Royal Commission held case study 34 on these schools in 2015.
cover: Brisbane Grammar quietly investigated complaints about counsellor Kevin Lynch in the early 1980s; he moved to St Paul's. A 2003 diocesan inquiry found Archbishop Hollingworth in 1993 allowed a known abuser to keep working as a priest.
cite: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane inquiry report, tabled May 2003; Royal Commission Case Study 34 (via Wikipedia 'Brisbane Grammar School', 'Peter Hollingworth')

n: Timothy Omotoso (Jesus Dominion International) — trafficking and rape charges ended in acquittal
who: Timothy Omotoso (Nigerian televangelist) and two co-accused
d: Omotoso was arrested on 20 April 2017 and charged with rape, human trafficking and racketeering, with prosecutors alleging he abused young women, some as young as 14. On 2 April 2025 the Eastern Cape High Court acquitted him and two co-accused, finding the prosecution had failed to prove guilt, citing prosecutorial mishandling. He was arrested on immigration grounds in May 2025.
cover: Whistleblower Pamela Mabini was shot dead outside her home on 7 March 2025, weeks before the verdict.
cite: Eastern Cape High Court, 2 April 2025 (via Wikipedia 'Timothy Omotoso')

n: T.B. Joshua (SCOAN) — BBC investigation into abuse of disciples
who: T.B. Joshua; Synagogue Church of All Nations (SCOAN)
d: A two-year BBC investigation published in January 2024 reported that more than 25 former followers alleged abuse by Joshua and the church over 15+ years, including rapes and forced abortions. One woman said he first raped her at 17. Joshua died in June 2021; the church denies the allegations. No official finding. Religious figure placed here for celebrity and political influence.
cite: BBC News investigation, Jan 2024 (via Wikipedia 'T. B. Joshua')

n: Bob Hewitt — tennis coach convicted of raping girls he coached
who: Bob Hewitt (Grand Slam doubles champion, coach)
d: On 23 March 2015 the South Gauteng High Court convicted former tennis champion Bob Hewitt of two rapes and one sexual assault of girls he coached in 1975–1982; he got an effective six years (appeal rejected 2016). The International Tennis Hall of Fame expelled him in 2016.
cite: South Gauteng High Court, 23 Mar 2015 (via Wikipedia 'Bob Hewitt')

n: Haitian Football Federation — Yves Jean-Bart banned by FIFA
who: Yves Jean-Bart (FHF president since 2000)
d: On 30 April 2020 Jean-Bart was accused of sexually abusing young female players at the federation's training centre; on 20 Nov 2020 FIFA's Ethics Committee banned him for life. Reports that the Court of Arbitration for Sport later annulled the ban (2023) could not be confirmed from an opened source in this pass, so status is set to 'alleged' pending check.
cite: FIFA Ethics Committee decision, 20 Nov 2020 (via Wikipedia 'Yves Jean-Bart')

n: Whyte Review — British Gymnastics
who: British Gymnastics
d: Anne Whyte KC's review, published June 2022, received more than 400 submissions describing sexual assault alongside emotional abuse and excessive weight control. Most of its findings concern non-sexual abuse; the sexual-abuse case count was not stated in the source opened.
cite: The Whyte Review, June 2022 (via Wikipedia 'Whyte Review')

n: Wrestling Federation of India — Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh (minor's complaint closed)
who: Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh (BJP MP, WFI president)
d: After Olympic wrestlers protested from January 2023, Delhi Police registered two FIRs on 28 April 2023, following Supreme Court intervention: one under the child-protection POCSO Act for a minor, one for six adult wrestlers. On 27 May 2025 a Delhi court cleared him in the minor's case. Charges were framed in the adult wrestlers' case, which continues (adults are outside this map's scope).
cite: Wikipedia 'Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh' (citing Indian Express, The Hindu)

n: Bibbiano ('Angeli e Demoni') — investigation into unlawful removal of children
who: Val d'Enza social services; mayor Andrea Carletti (house arrest 2019)
d: In June 2019 Italian police said they had uncovered a group accused of manipulating children's testimony to remove them from families and place them with foster parents; Bibbiano's mayor Andrea Carletti was placed under house arrest (confirmed Aug 2019). The trial outcomes for the defendants were NOT verified in this pass and must be checked before publication; this belongs more naturally in the 'adoption' setting.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bibbiano' (citing ANSA/press, June–Aug 2019)

n: Svay Pak child brothels — 2003 raid and later decline
who: Brothels in Svay Pak (mostly ethnic Vietnamese victims)
d: Brothels in Svay Pak, a village north of Phnom Penh, proliferated in the 1990s; in May 2000 there were 24 brothels with about 320 women on two streets, and in 2002 children, mostly ethnic Vietnamese sold by poor families, were exploited by Western child-sex tourists. A police raid in January 2003 after ministerial and ASEAN pressure was announced in advance. ABC News in 2017 found the share of children among those in sex work had fallen to 1–2% from 35%.
cover: The 22 January 2003 police raid was widely advertised in advance; almost all children had been moved and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had extorted brothel owners.
cite: Wikipedia 'Svay Pak' (citing Haugen 2005, Daily Telegraph, Dateline NBC, ABC News 2017)

n: Morocco — royal pardon of Spanish child rapist Daniel Galván (2013)
who: Daniel Galván Viña
d: Galván, a Spanish national living in Kenitra, was arrested in 2011 and sentenced to 30 years for raping at least eleven Moroccan children. On 30 July 2013 the king pardoned him as part of a gesture to Spain; after public outrage and protests, the pardon was cancelled on 4 August, the first such cancellation. Galván was arrested in Spain on 7 August on a Moroccan warrant; Spanish courts refused extradition.
cover: King Mohammed VI pardoned Galván on 30 July 2013 among 48 Spanish prisoners; he left Morocco on an expired passport with authorities' knowledge before the pardon was cancelled. Protesters in Rabat were violently dispersed. A 2010 US cable reported a 2006 royal pardon of a French man convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh.
cite: Wikipedia 'Daniel Galván scandal' (citing Lakome, El País, MAP); CNN, 4–6 Aug 2013

n: Kamathipura, Mumbai — red-light district fed by trafficking from Nepal and Indian states
who: Brothels of Kamathipura
d: Kamathipura in Mumbai grew into what has been called Asia's largest sex district; in recent decades large numbers of Nepalese women and girls were trafficked there, alongside women trafficked from other Indian states. The 2025 US TIP report says buyer concerns about brothels have pushed sex trafficking in India towards spas, hotels and private residences arranged by technology, and that India reported 204 convicted traffickers and 1,134 acquittals in its 2022 crime data.
cite: Wikipedia 'Kamathipura'; US TIP Report 2025 — India

n: Japan — 'JK business' and compensated dating (police survey 2024; US TIP 2025)
who: JK businesses, often with organized-crime ties
d: The 'JK business' sells simulated dates and services with high-school girls. A National Police Agency survey at the end of December 2024 counted 91 establishments advertising in this way, 70 per cent in Tokyo. Kanagawa first regulated it in 2011 and Tokyo enacted a dedicated ordinance in 2017. The 2025 US TIP report says JK variants and 'compensated dating', often tied to organized crime, continue to facilitate sex trafficking of Japanese children and of children from China, South Korea, Laos, the Philippines, Singapore and Vietnam.
cite: Wikipedia 'JK business' (citing National Police Agency); US TIP 2025 — Japan
